title: 26. Array Methods (Mutating)
theory:
Some methods modify the original array directly.
push(): adds to end.
pop(): removes from end.
unshift(): adds to start.
shift(): removes from start.
splice(): adds/removes from specific index.
code:
const arr = [1, 2];
arr.push(3); // [1,2,3]
arr.push(4); // [1,2,3,4]

arr.pop(); // removes 4

arr.unshift(0); // [0,1,2,3]
arr.shift(); // removes 0

// Splice (start, deleteCount, ...items)
arr.splice(1, 1, 99); // [1, 99, 3]

title: 27. Array Methods (Non-Mutating)
theory:
Methods that return a NEW array or value without changing the original.
slice(): extracts a portion.
concat(): merges arrays.
includes(): checks if value exists.
join(): converts to string.

title: 28. Higher-Order Array Methods: map()
theory:
Higher Order Functions take functions as arguments or return functions.
map() creates a NEW array by applying a callback function to every element in the original array. Great for data transformations.

title: 29. Higher-Order Array Methods: filter()
theory: filter() creates a NEW array containing only the elements that pass the test implemented by the provided callback function.

title: 30. Higher-Order Array Methods: reduce()
theory: reduce() executes a reducer callback function on each element, resulting in a single output value (e.g., summing all numbers). It passes the 'accumulator' to the next iteration.

title: 31. Objects Basics
theory:
Objects hold Key-Value pairs. Keys are strings (or symbols). Values can be anything (primitives, arrays, functions, other objects).
Dot notation and Bracket notation are used for access.

title: 32. Object Methods & 'this'
theory:
Functions inside objects are called Methods. The 'this' keyword inside a method refers to the object executing the method. 
Warning: Arrow functions DO NOT bind 'this'!

title: 33. Destructuring (ES6)
theory:
Destructuring assignment unpacks values from arrays, or properties from objects, into distinct variables.
It makes code cleaner and prevents repetitive dot notation.

title: 34. Spread & Rest Operators (...)
theory:
Spread (...) expands iterables into single elements (used for copying/merging). 
Rest (...) collects multiple elements and 'condenses' them into a single array (used in function parameters).

title: 35. DOM Introduction
output:
[Browser Output]
The DOM translates HTML tags into JS Objects.
theory: DOM (Document Object Model) is a programming interface for web documents. It represents the page so that programs can change the document structure, style, and content. The global object is `document`.

title: 36. Selecting DOM Elements
theory:
You need to select elements before modifying them.
getElementById(): Fast, returns single element.
querySelector(): Uses CSS selectors (.class, #id). returns first match.
querySelectorAll(): Returns a NodeList of all matches.

title: 37. Modifying DOM Content
theory:
innerText: Reads/writes rendered text only.
textContent: Reads/writes all text (even hidden).
innerHTML: Reads/writes HTML markup inside the element.

title: 38. DOM Styling & Classes
theory: You can change inline styles via element.style, but the best practice is to add/remove CSS classes using classList.

title: 39. DOM Events
theory: Events are actions that happen in the browser (click, submit, hover, keypress). Event Listeners wait for these actions and execute a callback function.

title: 40. Event Bubbling & Capturing
output:
[Click inner div]
> Inner Clicked
> Outer Clicked
theory:
When an event happens on an element, it first runs the handlers on it, then on its parent, then all the way up (Bubbling).
Capturing is the opposite (top to down).
Stop bubbling using e.stopPropagation().

title: 41. Event Delegation
theory: Instead of adding event listeners to 100 individual list items, you add ONE listener to their parent (<ul>). It uses Event Bubbling to catch clicks from children. Highly memory efficient!

title: 42. Creating Elements dynamically
theory: You can construct DOM elements entirely in JS memory and append them to the page using appendChild() or append().

title: 43. setTimeout & setInterval
theory:
Web APIs provided by the browser (not JS engine!).
setTimeout: Runs callback ONCE after delay.
setInterval: Runs callback REPEATEDLY every delay.

title: 44. The Event Loop
theory:
JS is single-threaded. How does it handle async tasks?
1. Async tasks (setTimeout, Fetch) are offloaded to Web APIs.
2. When finished, callbacks go to Callback Queue (or Microtask Queue for Promises).
3. Event Loop checks: If Call Stack is empty, it pushes the callback from Queue to Stack.

title: 45. Callback Hell (Pyramid of Doom)
theory: When you have multiple dependent async operations, you end up nesting callbacks inside callbacks. This makes the code horizontal, unreadable, and hard to debug. (Solution: Promises).

title: 46. Promises
theory:
A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion (or failure) of an async operation.
States: Pending, Fulfilled (Resolved), or Rejected.
Promises solve callback hell.

title: 47. Microtask Queue
theory:
Event loop handles two queues: Callback Queue (setTimeout) and Microtask Queue (Promises, MutationObserver).
Microtask Queue has HIGHER priority. Event loop empties it completely before moving to Callback Queue.

title: 48. Async / Await
theory: Introduced in ES8. Syntactic sugar over Promises. Makes async code look like synchronous code! 'await' pauses the execution of the async function until the promise settles.

title: 49. Error Handling (try...catch)
theory: When using async/await, we use standard try/catch blocks to handle errors (rejected promises). Without this, an error will crash the script.

title: 50. Fetch API
theory: The modern way to make HTTP requests (replacing old XMLHttpRequest). It returns a Promise. The response needs to be converted to JSON using response.json() (which is also a promise).
